summary.text: For \(n=27=3^3\), one has \(\Omega(27)=3\), but the Möbius sum reduces to \(a(27)=27!\,(H_{27}-H_9)>0\): the terms with quotients \(27\) and \(9\) vanish as nonsquarefree, leaving only the contributions from quotients \(3\) and \(1\). Thus \(27\) is a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j
\]
denote the \(n\)-th harmonic number. The defining relation for A067857 is
\[
\sum_{k\mid n}\frac{a(k)}{k!}=H_n.
\]
Set \(b(k)=a(k)/k!\). Then this relation says
\[
H_n=\sum_{k\mid n}b(k).
\]
By Möbius inversion,
\[
b(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)H_d,
\]
where \(\mu\) is the ordinary Möbius function. Consequently
\[
a(n)=n!\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)H_d. \tag{1}
\]

We disprove the conjecture using the positive integer
\[
n=27.
\]
The positive divisors of \(27\) are exactly
\[
1,3,9,27.
\]
The Möbius values needed in (1) are
\[
\mu(27)=0,\qquad \mu(9)=0,\qquad \mu(3)=-1,\qquad \mu(1)=1.
\]
Indeed, \(27=3^3\) and \(9=3^2\) are divisible by the square \(3^2\), so their Möbius values are zero; \(3\) is prime, so its Möbius value is \(-1\); and by definition \(\mu(1)=1\).

Applying (1) and considering each divisor separately therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(27)
&=27!\bigl(\mu(27)H_1+\mu(9)H_3+\mu(3)H_9+\mu(1)H_{27}\bigr)\\
&=27!\bigl(0\cdot H_1+0\cdot H_3-H_9+H_{27}\bigr)\\
&=27!(H_{27}-H_9).
\end{aligned}
\]
But
\[
H_{27}-H_9=\sum_{j=10}^{27}\frac1j.
\]
Every summand in this last expression is strictly positive, so \(H_{27}-H_9>0\). Since \(27!>0\), it follows that
\[
a(27)>0. \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, the rational arithmetic can also be made fully explicit:
\[
H_{27}-H_9=\frac{85332099113}{80313433200}>0,
\]
and hence
\[
a(27)=27!\frac{85332099113}{80313433200}
=11569298561272520297349120000>0.
\]
The exact value is not needed; its positive sign already follows from the sum of positive reciprocals.

On the other hand, because \(3\) is prime and
\[
27=3^3,
\]
the prime factorization of \(27\), with multiplicity, consists of the three factors \(3,3,3\). Thus
\[
\Omega(27)=3.
\]
In particular, \(\Omega(27)\) is odd and is at least \(3\). Therefore the right-hand side of the conjectured equivalence
\[
a(n)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\Omega(n)\text{ is odd and }\Omega(n)\ge 3\bigr)
\]
is true when \(n=27\). If the conjecture were correct, it would follow that \(a(27)<0\). This contradicts (2), which shows that \(a(27)>0\).

Hence \(n=27\) is a counterexample, and the proposed equivalence is false.
